problem:
The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ c\end{aligned}].
$$

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/3b195dda0cddb83bb414ff40ec076286765b7f599e1bac8cc7d04bdd6e9273e2.png)
examples.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $\mathbf{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $\mathbf T$ gives us the following information:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/ead1edec5d6fa82de8eb0137a838826221e0f45093782bc1b0a32111b05a37f4.png)

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{(-4)\cdot 7-(-9)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c = -7 + 3 + 8 = 4.
$$

feedback.problem:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}v-u \\ u+v\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u-2 \\ u-v+1\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3u+6v \\ u+2v-1\end{aligned}]$
feedback.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}v-u \\ u+v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-u+v \\ u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|=(-1)\cdot 1-1\cdot 1=-2\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-2 \\ u-v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u \\ u-v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|=1\cdot (-1)-0\cdot 1=-1\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{2}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u+6v \\ u+2v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u+6v \\ u+2v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|=3\cdot 2-6\cdot 1=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{3}$ is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{2}$ only."
